advanced-conditional-forms-a1.prompt: If I ___ (study) harder at university, I would have a better job now.
advanced-conditional-forms-a1.explanation: The past condition (didn't study) explaining a present result needs the past perfect: had studied.

advanced-conditional-forms-a2.prompt: ___ you need any assistance, don't hesitate to ask.
advanced-conditional-forms-a2.explanation: Conditional inversion for a less-likely future event drops “if” and fronts “Should.”

advanced-conditional-forms-a3.prompt: If it ___ (not/be) for her advice, I would have made a huge mistake.
advanced-conditional-forms-a3.explanation: “If it hadn't been for” needs the past perfect form “hadn't been,” not the present “isn't.”

advanced-conditional-forms-a4.prompt: ___ he arrived on time, he would have caught his connection.
advanced-conditional-forms-a4.explanation: Inversion of the third conditional fronts “Had” in place of “If he had.”

advanced-conditional-forms-a5.prompt: Were I ___ (be) in charge, I would change the whole policy.
advanced-conditional-forms-a5.explanation: The “Were + subject + to + infinitive” inversion pattern needs “to be” here, not “be” alone.

advanced-conditional-forms-a6.prompt: If she weren't so shy, she ___ (speak) up in the meeting yesterday.
advanced-conditional-forms-a6.explanation: “Yesterday” signals a past result, so the second-conditional “if” clause pairs with “would have spoken” — a mixed conditional.

advanced-conditional-forms-a7.prompt: But for the quick response of the paramedics, he ___ (not/survive).
advanced-conditional-forms-a7.explanation: “But for” + noun phrase functions like a third-conditional “if” clause, so the result needs “would have” + past participle.

advanced-conditional-forms-a8.prompt: Suppose you ___ (lose) your passport abroad — what would you do?
advanced-conditional-forms-a8.explanation: “Suppose” + past tense creates a present hypothetical, just like a second-conditional “if” clause.

advanced-conditional-forms-a9.prompt: Had they listened to the experts, the crisis ___ (avoid).
advanced-conditional-forms-a9.explanation: The inverted third-conditional “Had they listened…” needs a passive “would have been avoided” in the result.

advanced-conditional-forms-a10.prompt: If I ___ (not/be) allergic to cats, I would have one by now.
advanced-conditional-forms-a10.explanation: The second-conditional “if” clause uses “weren't” for all subjects, matching the present result “would have.”

advanced-conditional-forms-b1.prompt: If you need any help, just ask. → Should ___
answer: Should you need any help, just ask.
advanced-conditional-forms-b1.explanation: “Should” inversion drops “if” and fronts the modal: Should you need…
advanced-conditional-forms-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b2.prompt: If I had known about the traffic, I would have left earlier. → Had ___
answer: Had I known about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
advanced-conditional-forms-b2.explanation: “Had” inversion replaces “If I had known” with “Had I known.”
advanced-conditional-forms-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b3.prompt: If we were to lose this contract, the whole team would suffer. → Were ___
answer: Were we to lose this contract, the whole team would suffer.
advanced-conditional-forms-b3.explanation: “Were…to” inversion replaces “If we were to lose” with “Were we to lose.”
advanced-conditional-forms-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b4.prompt: If it hadn't been for the rain, the match would have finished. → But for ___
answer: But for the rain, the match would have finished.
advanced-conditional-forms-b4.explanation: “But for” + noun phrase replaces the whole “if it hadn't been for” clause.
advanced-conditional-forms-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b5.prompt: If she hadn't warned us, we would have walked into the trap. → If it hadn't ___
answer: If it hadn't been for her warning, we would have walked into the trap.
advanced-conditional-forms-b5.explanation: “If it hadn't been for” + noun phrase (her warning) replaces a clause built around a person's action.
advanced-conditional-forms-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b6.prompt: If you were to ask him, he would probably say yes. → Were ___
answer: Were you to ask him, he would probably say yes.
advanced-conditional-forms-b6.explanation: “Were…to” inversion replaces “If you were to ask” with “Were you to ask.”
advanced-conditional-forms-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-b7.prompt: If I had left earlier, I wouldn't be stuck in this traffic now. (identify: mixed or standard?) → rewrite keeping the same meaning with "Had..."
answer: Had I left earlier, I wouldn't be stuck in this traffic now.
advanced-conditional-forms-b7.explanation: “Had” inversion replaces “If I had left” with “Had I left,” keeping the mixed-conditional result unchanged.
advanced-conditional-forms-b7.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (use inversion or an alternative "if" structure)

advanced-conditional-forms-c1.incorrect: If I would have seen him, I would have said hello.
answer: If I had seen him, I would have said hello.
advanced-conditional-forms-c1.explanation: The if-clause never uses “would have” — use the past perfect “had seen.”

advanced-conditional-forms-c2.incorrect: Had she study harder, she would have passed.
answer: Had she studied harder, she would have passed.
advanced-conditional-forms-c2.explanation: The inverted “Had” clause needs the past participle “studied,” not the base form “study.”

advanced-conditional-forms-c3.incorrect: If it weren't for your support, I would have gave up.
answer: If it weren't for your support, I would have given up.
advanced-conditional-forms-c3.explanation: “Give” is irregular — the third-conditional result needs the past participle “given,” not “gave.”

advanced-conditional-forms-c4.incorrect: Were he to knows the truth, he would be furious.
answer: Were he to know the truth, he would be furious.
advanced-conditional-forms-c4.explanation: After “Were…to,” use the bare infinitive “know,” not “knows.”

advanced-conditional-forms-c5.incorrect: Should you needed anything, just let us know.
answer: Should you need anything, just let us know.
advanced-conditional-forms-c5.explanation: After “Should” in this inversion, use the bare infinitive “need,” not the past tense “needed.”

advanced-conditional-forms-c6.incorrect: If I was you, I would have accepted the offer.
answer: If I were you, I would have accepted the offer.
advanced-conditional-forms-c6.explanation: “Were,” not “was,” is standard for all subjects in this fixed hypothetical expression.

advanced-passive-structures-a1.prompt: The suspect ___ (believe / hide) somewhere near the border.

advanced-passive-structures-a2.prompt: All safety checks ___ (must / complete) before takeoff.

advanced-passive-structures-a5.prompt: The bridge ___ (should / repair) months ago, but nothing was done.
advanced-passive-structures-a5.explanation: An unfulfilled past obligation needs the modal perfect passive: should have been repaired.

advanced-passive-structures-a6.prompt: It ___ (report / that) the CEO resigned suddenly.
advanced-passive-structures-a6.explanation: The impersonal “It + is + reporting verb + that” pattern reports a claim without naming the source.

advanced-passive-structures-a7.prompt: He ___ (rumor / offer) a position at a rival firm.
answers: is rumored to have been offered
advanced-passive-structures-a7.explanation: A rumor about something already completed needs the perfect passive infinitive.

advanced-passive-structures-a8.prompt: Our tickets ___ (get / upgrade) at the last minute.
advanced-passive-structures-a8.explanation: A sudden, fortunate one-off event fits the get-passive.

advanced-passive-structures-a9.prompt: The results ___ (must / announce) by noon tomorrow.
advanced-passive-structures-a9.explanation: A present/future obligation uses modal + be + past participle.

advanced-passive-structures-a10.prompt: The painting ___ (allege / steal) from the museum in 1990.
answers: is alleged to have been stolen
advanced-passive-structures-a10.explanation: An allegation about a past event needs the perfect passive infinitive: alleged to have been stolen.

advanced-passive-structures-b1.prompt: People say that the company is losing money. → The company ___
answer: The company is said to be losing money.
advanced-passive-structures-b1.explanation: “Say” becomes “is said to be” + verb-ing for an ongoing situation.
advanced-passive-structures-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b2.prompt: They believe he escaped through the back door. → He ___
answer: He is believed to have escaped through the back door.
advanced-passive-structures-b2.explanation: “Believe” + an earlier action needs the perfect passive infinitive: believed to have escaped.
advanced-passive-structures-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b3.prompt: Everyone thinks the singer wrote the song herself. → The singer ___

advanced-passive-structures-b3.explanation: “Think” + an earlier action needs “thought to have written.”
advanced-passive-structures-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b4.prompt: People understood that the deal had fallen through. → It ___
answer: It was understood that the deal had fallen through.
advanced-passive-structures-b4.explanation: “Understand” reports a past belief with the impersonal “It was understood that…” pattern.
advanced-passive-structures-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b5.prompt: Journalists reported that the minister had lied. → The minister ___
answer: The minister is reported to have lied.
advanced-passive-structures-b5.explanation: “Report” + an earlier action needs “reported to have lied.”
advanced-passive-structures-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b6.prompt: They say the castle is haunted. → The castle ___
answer: The castle is said to be haunted.
advanced-passive-structures-b6.explanation: “Say” + an ongoing state needs “said to be haunted.”
advanced-passive-structures-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the passive reporting structure)

advanced-passive-structures-b7.prompt: People assume the twins are identical. → The twins ___
answer: The twins are assumed to be identical.
advanced-passive-structures-b7.explanation: “Assume” + a present state needs “assumed to be identical.”

advanced-passive-structures-c2.incorrect: He is said having escaped through the roof.

advanced-passive-structures-c2.explanation: The reporting passive needs “to have,” not “having,” for a completed action.

advanced-passive-structures-c3.incorrect: The proposal should approved before the deadline.
answer: The proposal should be approved before the deadline.
advanced-passive-structures-c3.explanation: The modal passive needs “be” between the modal and the past participle.

advanced-passive-structures-c4.incorrect: My phone got steal on the bus this morning.
answer: My phone got stolen on the bus this morning.
advanced-passive-structures-c4.explanation: The get-passive needs the past participle “stolen,” not the base form “steal.”

advanced-passive-structures-c5.incorrect: It is believe that the treaty will be signed soon.
answer: It is believed that the treaty will be signed soon.
advanced-passive-structures-c5.explanation: The reporting passive needs the past participle “believed,” not the base form.

advanced-passive-structures-c6.incorrect: The files must has been deleted by mistake.
answer: The files must have been deleted by mistake.
advanced-passive-structures-c6.explanation: After a modal, always use “have,” never “has,” even in the passive.

advanced-verb-patterns-a8.prompt: We got the roof ___ (repair) before winter.

advanced-verb-patterns-a9.prompt: He pretended ___ (not/notice) the mistake in the report.

advanced-verb-patterns-a10.prompt: Try ___ (restart) the router if the connection drops.

advanced-verb-patterns-b2.prompt: It's possible that he already left. He seems... → He seems ___

advanced-verb-patterns-b4.prompt: Someone is cutting our lawn every Friday now. (rewrite with a causative) → We get ___
answer: We get our lawn cut every Friday now.
advanced-verb-patterns-b4.explanation: “Get” + object + past participle is the more informal causative form.

advanced-verb-patterns-b5.prompt: I have a clear memory of visiting that castle as a child. → I remember ___
answer: I remember visiting that castle as a child.
advanced-verb-patterns-b5.explanation: “Remember” + gerund describes a memory of a completed action.

advanced-verb-patterns-b6.prompt: He paused his work in order to answer the phone. → He stopped ___
answer: He stopped to answer the phone.
advanced-verb-patterns-b6.explanation: “Stop” + to-infinitive means pausing one activity to do another.

advanced-verb-patterns-c1.incorrect: I remember to visit Paris when I was ten.
answer: I remember visiting Paris when I was ten.
advanced-verb-patterns-c1.explanation: “Remember” + gerund describes a memory of a completed action, not a task (to-infinitive).

advanced-verb-patterns-c2.incorrect: She stopped answering the door — I think she's finally home again.
answer: She stopped answering the door — I think she's finally home again.
advanced-verb-patterns-c2.explanation: This sentence is already correct as written — no error to fix; “stopped answering” (gerund) correctly describes a habit that ended.

advanced-verb-patterns-c3.incorrect: He claims meeting the queen once.
answer: He claims to have met the queen once.
advanced-verb-patterns-c3.explanation: “Claim” + perfect infinitive is needed to report an earlier event: claims to have met.

advanced-verb-patterns-c4.incorrect: I had my hair to cut yesterday.
answer: I had my hair cut yesterday.
advanced-verb-patterns-c4.explanation: The causative “have something done” needs the past participle “cut,” not a to-infinitive.

advanced-verb-patterns-c5.incorrect: They admitted to lose the documents last year.
answer: They admitted to having lost the documents last year.
advanced-verb-patterns-c5.explanation: “Admit to” + perfect gerund is needed to show the losing happened before the admission.

advanced-verb-patterns-c6.incorrect: Try to turning the dial slowly.
answer: Try turning the dial slowly.
advanced-verb-patterns-c6.explanation: “Try” + gerund (experimenting with a method) never takes “to” before the -ing form.

complex-noun-phrases-a1.prompt: The man ___ (who is sitting) in the corner is my old professor.
complex-noun-phrases-a1.explanation: A reduced relative clause for an active meaning (the man himself sits) drops “who is” and keeps the -ing form.
complex-noun-phrases-a1.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a2.prompt: Photos ___ (that were taken) during the trip are on my laptop.
complex-noun-phrases-a2.explanation: A reduced relative clause for a passive meaning (the photos were taken) drops “that were” and keeps the past participle.
complex-noun-phrases-a2.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a3.prompt: Employees ___ (who are working) overtime will be compensated.
complex-noun-phrases-a3.explanation: Active meaning (the employees themselves work) needs the -ing form.
complex-noun-phrases-a3.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a4.prompt: The bridge ___ (that was built) in 1930 is still in use today.
complex-noun-phrases-a4.explanation: Passive meaning (the bridge was built) needs the past participle.
complex-noun-phrases-a4.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a5.prompt: Anyone ___ (who is interested) in the position should apply by Friday.
complex-noun-phrases-a5.explanation: “Interested” functions here as a reduced passive participle (anyone who is interested).
complex-noun-phrases-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a6.prompt: The letter ___ (that was sent) last week never arrived.
complex-noun-phrases-a6.explanation: Passive meaning (the letter was sent) needs the past participle.
complex-noun-phrases-a6.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a7.prompt: Students ___ (who are studying) abroad often report culture shock.
complex-noun-phrases-a7.explanation: Active meaning (the students themselves study) needs the -ing form.
complex-noun-phrases-a7.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-a8.prompt: The car ___ (that was parked) outside was towed.
complex-noun-phrases-a8.explanation: Passive meaning (the car was parked) needs the past participle.
complex-noun-phrases-a8.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (reduce the relative clause or choose the correct participle)

complex-noun-phrases-b1.prompt: The city decided to build a new stadium. (rewrite starting with "The city's decision...")
answer: The city's decision to build a new stadium was welcomed by residents.
complex-noun-phrases-b1.explanation: “Decide” becomes the noun “decision” — nominalization turns the verb into the sentence's subject.
complex-noun-phrases-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-b2.prompt: They failed to reach an agreement, which frustrated everyone. (start with "Their failure...")
answer: Their failure to reach an agreement frustrated everyone.
complex-noun-phrases-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-b3.prompt: He was absent frequently, which concerned his teachers. (start with "His frequent absence...")
answer: His frequent absence concerned his teachers.
complex-noun-phrases-b3.explanation: “Absent” (adjective) becomes the noun “absence,” following possessive + adjective order: his frequent absence.
complex-noun-phrases-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-b4.prompt: She was promoted quickly, which surprised her colleagues. (start with "Her quick promotion...")
answer: Her quick promotion surprised her colleagues.
complex-noun-phrases-b4.explanation: “Promoted” becomes the noun “promotion,” following possessive + adjective order: her quick promotion.
complex-noun-phrases-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-b5.prompt: The prices increased suddenly, which shocked consumers. (start with "The sudden increase...")
answer: The sudden increase in prices shocked consumers.
complex-noun-phrases-b5.explanation: “Increased” becomes the noun “increase,” needing “in” before the following noun: increase in prices.
complex-noun-phrases-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-b6.prompt: They refused to comment, which raised suspicion. (start with "Their refusal...")
answer: Their refusal to comment raised suspicion.
complex-noun-phrases-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (turn the underlined verb/adjective into a noun — nominalization)

complex-noun-phrases-c1.incorrect: The team leading by Maria won the award.
answer: The team led by Maria won the award.
complex-noun-phrases-c1.explanation: A reduced relative clause for a passive meaning (the team was led) needs the past participle “led,” not “leading.”

complex-noun-phrases-c2.incorrect: The novel wrote by an unknown author became a bestseller.
answer: The novel written by an unknown author became a bestseller.
complex-noun-phrases-c2.explanation: Passive meaning (the novel was written) needs the past participle “written,” not the past simple “wrote.”

complex-noun-phrases-c3.incorrect: His refuse to apologize made things worse.
answer: His refusal to apologize made things worse.
complex-noun-phrases-c3.explanation: Nominalization needs the noun form “refusal,” not the bare verb “refuse.”

complex-noun-phrases-c4.incorrect: The workers affecting by the strike stayed home.
answer: The workers affected by the strike stayed home.
complex-noun-phrases-c4.explanation: Passive meaning (the workers were affected) needs the past participle “affected,” not “affecting.”

complex-noun-phrases-c5.incorrect: The results announcing yesterday shocked everyone.
answer: The results announced yesterday shocked everyone.
complex-noun-phrases-c5.explanation: Passive meaning (the results were announced) needs the past participle “announced,” not “announcing.”

complex-noun-phrases-c6.incorrect: Her improve in performance was noticeable.
answer: Her improvement in performance was noticeable.
complex-noun-phrases-c6.explanation: Nominalization needs the noun form “improvement,” not the bare verb “improve.”

csc1.prompt: ___ the traffic, we arrived right on time.
csc1.explanation: “Despite/in spite of” + noun expresses contrast without a full clause.
csc1.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc2.prompt: He whispered the plan ___ no one would overhear.
csc2.explanation: “So that” + clause expresses purpose when the subject can take a modal (would).
csc2.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc3.prompt: It was ___ a long meeting that people started checking their phones.
csc3.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” for a result clause with a noun.
csc3.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc4.prompt: The coffee here is excellent, ___ the tea is rather weak.
csc4.explanation: “Whereas” neutrally contrasts two facts side by side.
csc4.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc5.prompt: She left the party early ___ catch the last train.
csc5.explanation: “So as to” / “in order to” + bare infinitive express purpose formally.
csc5.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc6.prompt: The instructions were ___ confusing that nobody followed them correctly.
csc6.explanation: “So” + adjective alone + “that” for a result clause without a noun.
csc6.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc7.prompt: He trained every day ___ improve his stamina.
csc7.explanation: Purpose clause with a bare infinitive.
csc7.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc8.prompt: ___ having a fever, she still went to work.
csc8.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc9.prompt: He spoke slowly and clearly ___ everyone in the room could understand.
csc9.explanation: “So that” + clause with a modal (could) for purpose.
csc9.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc10.prompt: It was ___ a generous offer that we couldn't refuse it.
csc10.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” for a result clause with a noun.
csc10.exerciseInstructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

csc11.prompt: He is rich, but he lives very simply. (rewrite with “whereas”)
answer: He is rich, whereas he lives very simply.
csc11.explanation: “Whereas” replaces “but” to contrast the two facts formally.
csc11.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc12.prompt: She failed the exam, but she didn't lose confidence. (rewrite with “even though”)
answer: Even though she failed the exam, she didn't lose confidence.
csc12.explanation: “Even though” opens the clause with the surprising fact.
csc12.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc13.prompt: He turned down the promotion. He wanted more free time. (join with “in order to”)
answer: He turned down the promotion in order to have more free time.
csc13.explanation: “In order to” + bare infinitive expresses his purpose.
csc13.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc14.prompt: It rained heavily. We still finished the hike. (join with “despite”)
answer: Despite the heavy rain, we still finished the hike.
csc14.explanation: “Despite” + noun phrase replaces the first sentence.
csc14.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc15.prompt: The test was extremely hard. Nobody finished it in time. (join with “so...that”)
answer: The test was so hard that nobody finished it in time.
csc15.explanation: “So” + adjective + “that” shows the result of the degree.
csc15.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc16.prompt: He apologized publicly. He wanted to repair his reputation. (join with “so that”)
answer: He apologized publicly so that he could repair his reputation.
csc16.explanation: “So that” + clause with “could” expresses his purpose.
csc16.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc17.prompt: It was a very persuasive speech. It changed several votes. (join with “such...that”)
answer: It was such a persuasive speech that it changed several votes.
csc17.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” shows the result.
csc17.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

csc18.incorrect: Despite he arrived late, no one seemed to mind.
answer: Despite arriving late, no one seemed to mind.
Although he arrived late, no one seemed to mind.
csc18.explanation: “Despite” needs a noun/gerund, not a subject + verb clause — use “although” if you want a full clause.

csc19.incorrect: It was so an emotional film that everyone cried.
answer: It was such an emotional film that everyone cried.

csc20.incorrect: She practiced every day so as she could improve faster.
answer: She practiced every day so as to improve faster.
She practiced every day so that she could improve faster.
csc20.explanation: “So as to” takes an infinitive, not a clause; use “so that” for a full clause.

csc21.incorrect: Whereas I respect his opinion, but I think he's wrong.
answer: Whereas I respect his opinion, I think he's wrong.
csc21.explanation: Don't combine “whereas” with “but” — the contrast is already built into “whereas.”

csc22.incorrect: The meeting was such long that we had to order dinner.
answer: The meeting was so long that we had to order dinner.
csc22.explanation: “So” goes with an adjective alone; there's no noun here.

csc23.incorrect: In spite of he lost the match, he stayed positive.
answer: In spite of losing the match, he stayed positive.
Although he lost the match, he stayed positive.
csc23.explanation: “In spite of” needs a noun/gerund, not a subject + verb clause.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a1.prompt: It ___ my brother who fixed the car, not me.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a1.explanation: The it-cleft frame is “It + was + emphasized element + who/that…” — “was” fills the verb slot.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a2.prompt: What really impressed the judges ___ her confidence on stage.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a2.explanation: A pseudo-cleft (“What…”) is followed by “be” before the emphasized element.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a3.prompt: It was ___ the noise, not the crowd, that bothered him most.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a3.explanation: The emphasized element sits right after “It was,” before “that.”

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a4.prompt: The reason she left early ___ to catch her flight.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a4.explanation: The “The reason…” pseudo-cleft is followed by “be” before the emphasized element (the purpose).

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a5.prompt: All he wants ___ a quiet place to work.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a5.explanation: The all-cleft uses “be” (here, present “is”) before the emphasized element.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a6.prompt: It was only when I moved abroad ___ I understood my parents better.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a6.explanation: The it-cleft's second clause is introduced by “that” after the emphasized time expression.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a7.prompt: What we should focus on ___ the customer experience, not just the price.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a7.explanation: The pseudo-cleft “What we should focus on…” is followed by “be” before the emphasized element.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a8.prompt: It ___ during the interview, not the written test, that he stood out.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-a8.explanation: The it-cleft frame needs “was” before the emphasized time expression.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b1.prompt: Her attitude, not her skills, worried the manager. (it-cleft)
answer: It was her attitude, not her skills, that worried the manager.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b1.explanation: The it-cleft frame “It was X, not Y, that…” puts the emphasized contrast right after “It was.”
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b2.prompt: I really admire his patience. (pseudo-cleft with "What")
answer: What I really admire is his patience.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b2.explanation: The pseudo-cleft “What I really admire is…” moves the emphasized element to the end.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b3.prompt: We met in Barcelona, not Madrid. (it-cleft)
answer: It was in Barcelona, not Madrid, that we met.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b3.explanation: The it-cleft frame emphasizes the place: “It was in Barcelona… that we met.”
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b4.prompt: She wants nothing more than some recognition. (all-cleft)
answer: All she wants is some recognition.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b4.explanation: The all-cleft “All she wants is…” emphasizes the one thing she wants.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b5.prompt: His lack of preparation caused the failure. (pseudo-cleft with "What")
answer: What caused the failure was his lack of preparation.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b5.explanation: The pseudo-cleft “What caused the failure was…” moves the cause to the end for emphasis.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b6.prompt: I called to apologize, not to argue. (it-cleft, emphasizing the reason)
answer: It was to apologize, not to argue, that I called.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b6.explanation: The it-cleft frame emphasizes the reason: “It was to apologize… that I called.”
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence as a cleft sentence, emphasizing the underlined part)

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c1.incorrect: It was John that he lost the keys.
answer: It was John who lost the keys.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c1.explanation: Use “who” (for a person) right after the emphasized element — don't add “that he.”

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c2.incorrect: What I need it is more time.
answer: What I need is more time.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c2.explanation: Don't add a redundant object pronoun (“it”) — the wh-clause already functions as the subject.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c3.incorrect: All what matters to her is her family.
answer: All that matters to her is her family.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c3.explanation: “All” already functions like “the only thing that” — use “that,” not “what,” after it.

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c4.incorrect: It the manager was who approved the budget.
answer: It was the manager who approved the budget.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c4.explanation: The it-cleft frame is “It + was + emphasized element + who/that,” not “It + emphasized element + was.”

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c5.incorrect: What surprised us it was the ending of the film.
answer: What surprised us was the ending of the film.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c5.explanation: Use “was” directly — don't duplicate the subject with a contracted “it was.”

emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c6.incorrect: It was not the price the thing that bothered me.
answer: It was not the price but the way it was handled that bothered me.
emphatic-and-stylistic-structures-c6.explanation: A negative contrast (“not X but Y”) needs both halves stated, not a vague “the thing that.”

future-forms-with-nuance-a1.prompt: He ___ (leave) the room when the lights suddenly went out.
future-forms-with-nuance-a1.explanation: “Was about to” + bare infinitive shows something on the brink of happening, interrupted here by the lights going out.
future-forms-with-nuance-a1.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a2.prompt: She had no idea that this trip ___ (change) her outlook on life.
future-forms-with-nuance-a2.explanation: Future-in-the-past “would” reports what was still to come, viewed from her past perspective.
future-forms-with-nuance-a2.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a3.prompt: We ___ (visit) the museum, but it was closed for renovation.
future-forms-with-nuance-a3.explanation: “Were going to” signals a plan that didn't happen (the museum was closed).
future-forms-with-nuance-a3.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a4.prompt: The young painter, still unknown at the time, ___ (become) world-famous within a decade.
future-forms-with-nuance-a4.explanation: “Would” (future-in-the-past) narrates an inevitable future event, without any sense of failure.
future-forms-with-nuance-a4.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a5.prompt: I ___ (call) you, but my phone died before I could.
future-forms-with-nuance-a5.explanation: “Was going to” signals an unfulfilled plan — the phone died first.
future-forms-with-nuance-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a6.prompt: He promised that he ___ (write) every week while he was away.
future-forms-with-nuance-a6.explanation: Inside a past narrative, a promised future action needs “would,” not “will.”
future-forms-with-nuance-a6.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a7.prompt: Just as she ___ (open) the letter, the phone rang.
future-forms-with-nuance-a7.explanation: “Was about to” + bare infinitive marks the interrupted moment, right as the phone rang.
future-forms-with-nuance-a7.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-a8.prompt: They ___ (get married) that summer, but the wedding was postponed.
future-forms-with-nuance-a8.explanation: “Were going to” signals a plan that changed — the wedding was postponed.
future-forms-with-nuance-a8.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (was/were going to, would, was/were about to, was/were to)

future-forms-with-nuance-b1.prompt: His plan was to open a restaurant, but he never did. (use "was going to")
answer: He was going to open a restaurant, but he never did.
future-forms-with-nuance-b1.explanation: “Was going to” + bare infinitive reports an unfulfilled plan.
future-forms-with-nuance-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-b2.prompt: At the time, nobody knew that the invention would change the world. (rewrite with "would," keeping the meaning)
answer: At the time, nobody knew that the invention would change the world.
future-forms-with-nuance-b2.explanation: “Would” (future-in-the-past) reports what was still to come, from a past vantage point.
future-forms-with-nuance-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-b3.prompt: I was on the verge of leaving when I heard the news. (rewrite with "was about to")
answer: I was about to leave when I heard the news.
future-forms-with-nuance-b3.explanation: “Was about to” + bare infinitive replaces “on the verge of” for an interrupted moment.
future-forms-with-nuance-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-b4.prompt: It was later revealed that the two rivals would become close friends. (rewrite with "were to")
answer: It was later revealed that the two rivals were to become close friends.
future-forms-with-nuance-b4.explanation: “Were to” (formal/literary) reports an event later revealed as fated or destined.
future-forms-with-nuance-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-b5.prompt: She planned to quit her job that year, but she got a promotion instead. (use "was going to")
answer: She was going to quit her job that year, but she got a promotion instead.
future-forms-with-nuance-b5.explanation: “Was going to” + bare infinitive reports a plan that changed.
future-forms-with-nuance-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-b6.prompt: We were on the point of signing the contract when the deal collapsed. (rewrite with "were about to")
answer: We were about to sign the contract when the deal collapsed.
future-forms-with-nuance-b6.explanation: “Were about to” + bare infinitive replaces “on the point of” for an interrupted moment.
future-forms-with-nuance-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the underlined idea using future-in-the-past)

future-forms-with-nuance-c1.incorrect: She was going to visited her grandmother, but it snowed all week.
answer: She was going to visit her grandmother, but it snowed all week.
future-forms-with-nuance-c1.explanation: “Was going to” is always followed by the bare infinitive “visit,” not the past form “visited.”

future-forms-with-nuance-c2.incorrect: He didn't realize that this mistake will cost him his job.
answer: He didn't realize that this mistake would cost him his job.
future-forms-with-nuance-c2.explanation: Inside a past narrative, future-in-the-past needs “would,” not “will.”

future-forms-with-nuance-c3.incorrect: I were about to leave when the taxi arrived.
answer: I was about to leave when the taxi arrived.

modality-with-nuance-c2.incorrect: You should have not ignored his advice.

modality-with-nuance-c3.incorrect: He can has forgotten the password.

advanced-discourse-devices-c2.incorrect: The plan is flawed, nevertheless we should still consider it.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-a6.explanation: “Did” substitutes for the whole action (waited), already clear from context.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b2.prompt: He hasn't decided yet, but he will decide soon.
answer: He hasn't decided yet, but he will soon.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b3.prompt: She was reading while she was waiting for the train.
answer: She was reading while waiting for the train.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b3.explanation: Omitting the repeated subject + auxiliary (“she was”) after “while” tightens the sentence.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each pair using ellipsis or substitution to avoid repetition)

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b4.prompt: The first experiment succeeded. The second experiment succeeded too.
answer: The first experiment succeeded, and so did the second.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b4.explanation: “So did” substitutes for the repeated verb phrase “succeeded.”
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each pair using ellipsis or substitution to avoid repetition)

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b5.prompt: If you want a coffee, take a coffee from the machine.
answer: If you want a coffee, take one from the machine.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b5.explanation: Indefinite “one” substitutes for “a coffee,” avoiding the repeated noun.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each pair using ellipsis or substitution to avoid repetition)

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b6.prompt: He told me to relax, and I relaxed.
answer: He told me to relax, and I did.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b6.explanation: “Did” substitutes for the whole action (relaxed), already clear from context.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-b6.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each pair using ellipsis or substitution to avoid repetition)

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c1.incorrect: She likes hiking, and her friend does it too.
answer: She likes hiking, and her friend does too.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c1.explanation: “Does too” already functions as the substitute verb phrase — adding “it” creates redundancy.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c2.incorrect: While she was cooking, was listening to music.
answer: While cooking, she was listening to music.
While she was cooking, she was listening to music.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c2.explanation: If you omit the subject after “while,” you must also omit the auxiliary (“was”) — ellipsis applies to both together.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c3.incorrect: He asked me to stop, and I did so it.
answer: He asked me to stop, and I did so.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c3.explanation: “Did so” already replaces the whole verb phrase — don't add another object (“it”) after it.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c4.incorrect: If you need a towel, take the one from the shelf. (no towel mentioned before)
answer: If you need a towel, take one from the shelf.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c4.explanation: “One” (indefinite substitution) is for an unspecified item; “the one” implies something already identified.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c5.incorrect: He hasn't replied yet, but he will do it tomorrow.
answer: He hasn't replied yet, but he will soon.
...but he will do so tomorrow.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c5.explanation: Use the bare auxiliary or “do so,” not “will do it,” which is redundant here.

complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c6.incorrect: The first plan failed; the second plan did the same it.
answer: The first plan failed; the second did the same.
complex-ellipsis-and-substitution-c6.explanation: “Did the same” already replaces the whole action — don't add another object (“it”) after it.

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a1.prompt: Every Sunday, my grandfather ___ (take) us fishing at dawn.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a1.explanation: “Would” works here because “take us fishing” is a repeated action, not a state — “used to” also works.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a1.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a2.prompt: He's ___ (always/complain) about the weather, no matter what it's like.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a2.explanation: Continuous + “always” adds a tone of complaint/irritation, not just a neutral habit.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a2.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a3.prompt: By the time the film starts, we ___ (already/eat) dinner.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a3.explanation: “By the time” + a completed future action needs the future perfect.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a3.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a4.prompt: So there I ___ (stand), completely frozen, when the alarm goes off.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a4.explanation: Historic present: switching to the present tense mid-narrative makes a past event feel immediate.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a4.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a5.prompt: The conference ___ (begin) at nine sharp tomorrow, according to the schedule.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a5.explanation: The simple present states a fixed schedule or timetable, even for a future event.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a5.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a6.prompt: She ___ (live) in Paris for a decade before she finally moved back home.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a6.explanation: The past perfect marks the action that happened before another past action (“moved back”).
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a6.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a7.prompt: As a teenager, I ___ (spend/would) hours reading in my room. (identify if "would" fits — rewrite if not)
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a7.explanation: “Spend hours reading” is a repeated action, not a state, so “would” fits here (unlike states such as have/be/know).
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a7.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a8.prompt: By the end of this year, they ___ (be) married for twenty years.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a8.explanation: A duration completed by a future point (“by the end of this year … twenty years”) needs the future perfect.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a8.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a9.prompt: He ___ (constantly/change) his mind, which drives the whole team crazy.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a9.explanation: Continuous + “constantly” frames the habit as irritating, not a neutral fact.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a9.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a10.prompt: Looking back now, I ___ (never/realize) how young we all were.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a10.explanation: Past perfect gives retrospective distance — looking back from a later point at an earlier lack of understanding.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-a10.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c1.incorrect: When I was young, I would live in a small village.
answer: When I was young, I lived in a small village.
When I was young, I used to live in a small village.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c1.explanation: “Would” can't describe a past state like living somewhere — use the simple past or “used to.”
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c1.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c2.incorrect: She always is checking her phone during meetings.
answer: She's always checking her phone during meetings.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c2.explanation: With “always” for irritation, use the continuous, and place “always” between the auxiliary and main verb.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c2.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c3.incorrect: Tomorrow at this time, I will finish the marathon.
answer: Tomorrow at this time, I will be finishing the marathon.
Tomorrow at this time, I will have finished the marathon.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c3.explanation: “Tomorrow at this time” needs an aspect that shows the marathon is still in progress or already done, not the simple future.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c3.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c4.incorrect: I had never saw such a beautiful sunset before that trip.
answer: I had never seen such a beautiful sunset before that trip.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c4.explanation: The past perfect needs the past participle (“seen”), not the simple past form (“saw”).
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c4.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c5.incorrect: By 2030, this company will produce twice as much as it does now, they predict. (identify tense issue and fix)
answer: By 2030, this company will be producing twice as much as it does now, they predict.
By 2030, this company will produce twice as much as it does now, they predict.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c5.explanation: A state still ongoing at a specific future point favors the future continuous over the simple future.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c5.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c6.incorrect: He's constantly forgets where he left his keys.
answer: He's constantly forgetting where he left his keys.
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c6.explanation: Continuous + “constantly” needs “is” + verb-ing, not the simple present “forgets.”
full-command-of-tenses-and-aspects-c6.lessonTitle: Full Command of All Tenses and Aspects

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a1.prompt: Gone ___ (be) the days when a college degree guaranteed a job.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a1.explanation: “Gone” fronts the sentence, inverting to “are” + subject (the days).

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a2.prompt: So fierce ___ (be) the debate that the session ran two hours over.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a2.explanation: “So + adjective” fronts the sentence, inverting to “was” + subject.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a2.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a3.prompt: Such ___ (be) the demand that tickets sold out within minutes.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a3.explanation: “Such” as a fronted intensifier triggers full inversion: “was” + subject.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a3.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a4.prompt: Deep in the valley ___ (lie) a village untouched by modern development.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a4.explanation: A fronted place adverbial (“Deep in the valley”) inverts to verb + subject: lies/lay a village.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a4.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a5.prompt: Equally important ___ (be) the need for transparency in government.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a5.explanation: A fronted “Equally important” inverts to “is” + subject.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a6.prompt: Never before ___ (the team / face) such intense scrutiny.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a6.explanation: “Never before” fronts the sentence, inverting to “had” + subject + past participle.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a6.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a7.prompt: Down ___ (come) the curtain, marking the end of the performance.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a7.explanation: A fronted adverbial of manner/place (“Down”) inverts to verb + subject: came the curtain.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a7.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a8.prompt: What truly matters ___ (be) the impact we leave behind, not the titles we hold.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a8.explanation: The pseudo-cleft “What truly matters” is followed directly by “is,” with no redundant “it.”
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-a8.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correctly inverted form)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b1.prompt: The days when people trusted the government blindly are over. (rewrite with "Gone are...")
answer: Gone are the days when people trusted the government blindly.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b1.explanation: “Gone are” fronts the sentence, inverting to “are” + subject (the days).
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the inversion or cleft structure indicated)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b2.prompt: Her speech was so powerful that the entire room stood and applauded. (rewrite with "So powerful was...")
answer: So powerful was her speech that the entire room stood and applauded.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b2.explanation: “So + adjective + was” inverts to put the subject (her speech) after “was.”
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the inversion or cleft structure indicated)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b3.prompt: The protest was so intense that the government was forced to respond. (rewrite with "Such was...")
answer: Such was the intensity of the protest that the government was forced to respond.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b3.explanation: “Such was” inverts to put the subject (the intensity) after “was.”
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the inversion or cleft structure indicated)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b4.prompt: Not authority but empathy truly defines a leader. (rewrite as a pseudo-cleft with "What...")
answer: What truly defines a leader is not authority, but empathy.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b4.explanation: The pseudo-cleft “What truly defines a leader is…” moves the emphasized contrast to the end.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the inversion or cleft structure indicated)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b5.prompt: An old lighthouse stood at the edge of the cliff. (rewrite fronting the place phrase and inverting)
answer: At the edge of the cliff stood an old lighthouse.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b5.explanation: A fronted place adverbial inverts to verb + subject: stood an old lighthouse.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite using the inversion or cleft structure indicated)

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c1.incorrect: Gone the certainty is that once defined our industry.
answer: Gone is the certainty that once defined our industry.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c1.explanation: The inversion after “Gone” requires “is” immediately after it, before the subject.

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c2.incorrect: So great her disappointment was that she left without a word.
answer: So great was her disappointment that she left without a word.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c2.explanation: After a fronted “So + adjective,” the verb (“was”) must come before the subject — full inversion.

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c3.incorrect: What truly matters it is how we treat one another.
answer: What truly matters is how we treat one another.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c3.explanation: The “what” clause already functions as the subject — adding “it” duplicates it unnecessarily.

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c4.incorrect: Deep in the archive documents lay forgotten for decades.
answer: Deep in the archive lay documents forgotten for decades.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c4.explanation: After the fronted adverbial of place, the verb (“lay”) comes before the subject (“documents”), not embedded mid-phrase.

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c5.incorrect: Such was outcry that the board resigned.
answer: Such was the outcry that the board resigned.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c5.explanation: “Such” as a fronted intensifier also triggers full inversion — verb before subject.

high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c6.incorrect: Never before the country had seen such unity.
answer: Never before had the country seen such unity.
high-level-clefts-and-inversions-c6.explanation: “Never before” fronts the sentence, so the auxiliary (“had”) inverts before the subject.

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a1.prompt: The theory, ___ was first proposed decades ago, has recently gained new support.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a1.explanation: Non-defining relative clause (marked by commas) referring to a thing (“theory”) — always “which,” never “that.”
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a1.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a2.prompt: The report ___ she submitted last week contained several errors. (defining, no comma — leave blank, or use “that”)
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a2.explanation: In a defining relative clause, the pronoun can be dropped when it's the object of its own clause (“the report she submitted”), or you can keep “that.”
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a2.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a3.prompt: Her argument, ___ few could refute, changed the course of the debate.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a3.explanation: Same non-defining pattern: a comma-set-off clause referring to a thing (“argument”) needs “which,” not “that.”
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a3.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a4.prompt: The findings ___ the team published were later called into question. (leave blank, or use “that”)
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a4.explanation: Same object-relative-pronoun omission as above: “findings” is the object of “published,” so the pronoun is optional (or use “that”).
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a4.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a5.prompt: The policy, ___ had been in place for over a decade, was finally repealed.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a5.explanation: Non-defining again — “which” is required here and can never be omitted, whether it's the subject or object of its own clause.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c1.incorrect: The proposal, that had taken months to draft, was rejected in minutes.
answer: The proposal, which had taken months to draft, was rejected in minutes.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c1.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (set off by commas) need “which” for things, never “that.”

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c2.incorrect: Although the evidence was strong, but the jury hesitated.
answer: Although the evidence was strong, the jury hesitated.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c2.explanation: “Although” already introduces the contrast — don't also add “but”; use one or the other, not both.

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c3.incorrect: Having finished the analysis, the results were presented by the team.
answer: Having finished the analysis, the team presented the results.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c3.explanation: The subject right after a participle clause must be the one performing that action — here, the team, not the results.

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c4.incorrect: The decline, that experts had predicted for years, finally arrived.
answer: The decline, which experts had predicted for years, finally arrived.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c4.explanation: Same rule as above: a comma-separated non-defining clause referring to a thing needs “which,” not “that.”

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c5.incorrect: What seemed impossible at first, it became routine within months.
answer: What seemed impossible at first became routine within months.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c5.explanation: A fronted “what”-clause acting as the subject takes no comma before the main verb, and doesn't need a redundant “it” repeating the subject.

highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c6.incorrect: The scandal, which it destroyed his career, was never fully explained.
answer: The scandal, which destroyed his career, was never fully explained.
highly-complex-sentence-architecture-c6.explanation: Don't repeat the subject with “it” once “which” is already doing that job as the clause's subject.

mastery-of-register-a1.prompt: (Legal) The Tenant ___ (will/shall) vacate the premises by the end of the lease term.
mastery-of-register-a1.explanation: Legal register uses “shall” for binding obligation, not the more casual “will.”

mastery-of-register-a2.prompt: (Academic) The findings ___ (show/kinda show) a clear pattern across all groups studied.
mastery-of-register-a2.explanation: Academic register avoids casual intensifiers like “kinda” — use the plain verb.
mastery-of-register-a2.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose the word/phrase that fits the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-a3.prompt: (Journalistic) The company confirmed the layoffs ___ (in a statement/basically) released on Friday.
mastery-of-register-a3.explanation: Journalistic register attributes claims formally (“in a statement”), not with a vague casual filler.
mastery-of-register-a3.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose the word/phrase that fits the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-a4.prompt: (Casual) ___ (I regret to inform you/Sorry), I can't make it tonight.
mastery-of-register-a4.explanation: Casual register favors short, direct phrasing over an inflated formal opener.
mastery-of-register-a4.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose the word/phrase that fits the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-a5.prompt: (Technical) ___ (Please consider disconnecting/Disconnect) the power source before opening the case.
mastery-of-register-a5.explanation: Technical/instructional register uses direct imperatives, not hedged suggestions.
mastery-of-register-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (choose the word/phrase that fits the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-b1.prompt: "The plan didn't work out." → Rewrite in academic register.
answer: The plan did not achieve its intended outcomes.
mastery-of-register-b1.explanation: Academic register replaces the casual verb phrase with a more formal, precise one: did not achieve its intended outcomes.
mastery-of-register-b1.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the sentence in the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-b2.prompt: "The tenant needs to pay rent by the 1st of the month or else." → Rewrite in legal register.
answer: The Tenant shall remit rent payment no later than the first day of each calendar month; failure to do so shall constitute a breach of this Agreement.
mastery-of-register-b2.explanation: Legal register uses “shall,” formal defined terms, and explicit consequences for breach.
mastery-of-register-b2.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the sentence in the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-b3.prompt: "The mayor said the roads will be fixed soon." → Rewrite in journalistic register (add attribution/lead style).
answer: The roads will be repaired soon, the mayor said on Tuesday.
mastery-of-register-b3.explanation: Journalistic register fronts the key fact and adds clear attribution (“the mayor said”).
mastery-of-register-b3.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the sentence in the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-b4.prompt: "One must exercise caution when the device is in operation." → Rewrite in casual register.
answer: Careful — this thing's running, so watch out.
mastery-of-register-b4.explanation: Casual register uses contractions, short clauses and direct address.
mastery-of-register-b4.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the sentence in the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-b5.prompt: "We think the marketing campaign kind of failed." → Rewrite in academic register.
answer: It could be argued that the marketing campaign did not meet its objectives.
mastery-of-register-b5.explanation: Academic register replaces “we think… kind of” with the hedged, impersonal “it could be argued that… did not meet its objectives.”
mastery-of-register-b5.exerciseInstructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite the sentence in the register indicated)

mastery-of-register-c1.incorrect: (Legal contract) The Buyer will maybe pay within 30 days.
answer: The Buyer shall pay within thirty (30) days.
mastery-of-register-c1.explanation: Legal register needs “shall,” not the hedged “will maybe,” for binding obligation.

mastery-of-register-c2.incorrect: (Academic essay) I feel like the evidence is pretty convincing, honestly.
answer: The evidence appears to be convincing.
mastery-of-register-c2.explanation: Academic register avoids first-person opinion markers (“I feel like”) and casual intensifiers (“pretty,” “honestly”).

mastery-of-register-c3.incorrect: (Technical manual) You might want to think about turning off the machine before cleaning it.
answer: Turn off the machine before cleaning it.
mastery-of-register-c3.explanation: Technical/instructional register uses a direct imperative, not a hedged suggestion (“you might want to think about”).

mastery-of-register-c4.incorrect: (Journalism) It is alleged, allegedly, according to some reports, that the CEO may have resigned.
answer: The CEO is reported to have resigned, according to sources.
mastery-of-register-c4.explanation: Journalistic style avoids redundant hedging/attribution stacked together — attribute once, clearly.

mastery-of-register-c5.incorrect: (Casual text to a friend) I regret to inform you that I am running late.
answer: Running late, sorry!
mastery-of-register-c5.explanation: Casual register favors short, direct phrasing over an overly formal opener.

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a1.prompt: It would ___ (seem) that the plan has stalled entirely.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a1.explanation: “It would seem that” is the fixed hedging frame — “seem” completes it.

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a2.prompt: She might ___ (well) be correct, but I'd like more evidence.

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a3.prompt: ___ I suggest we postpone the decision until next week? (very formal request)

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a4.prompt: He ___ (might/expect) to know better, given his experience.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a4.explanation: “Might have been expected to” (passive) shows others expected it of him, with a layer of uncertainty.

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a4.lessonTitle: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a5.prompt: There is reason ___ (believe) the figures were manipulated.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a5.explanation: “There is reason to” + bare infinitive is the fixed epistemic frame.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a5.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct modal/epistemic phrase)
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a5.lessonTitle: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a6.prompt: It ___ (stand/reason) that demand would fall as prices rose.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a6.explanation: “It stands to reason that” is the fixed idiom for a logical inference.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a6.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct modal/epistemic phrase)
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a6.lessonTitle: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a7.prompt: One cannot ___ (rule out) the possibility of further delays.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a7.explanation: “Cannot rule out” is the fixed phrase for an epistemic possibility that can't be excluded.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a7.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct modal/epistemic phrase)
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a7.lessonTitle: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude

native-like-modality-and-attitude-a8.prompt: She should, in theory, ___ (already/inform) of the changes.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a8.explanation: The passive perfect (“have been informed”) shows the informing was done by someone else, by now.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a8.exerciseInstructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct modal/epistemic phrase)
native-like-modality-and-attitude-a8.lessonTitle: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude

native-like-modality-and-attitude-b1.prompt: The results are wrong. (make it tentative/hedged)
answer: It would seem that the results are incorrect.
native-like-modality-and-attitude-b1.explanation: “It would seem that” softens the direct claim into a hedge.
